items.title: 2.4 Graph of the Cube Root Function

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The basic cube root function is \(y = \sqrt[3]{x}\): \(\sqrt[3]{x}\) is the number whose cube is \(x\). Every real number has exactly one real cube root, including negatives: \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\), \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\), \(\sqrt[3]{0} = 0\). So its domain and range are both all real numbers.
In \(y = \sqrt[3]{x - 1}\) the "\(-1\)" inside moves the whole graph one unit to the right: the centre point \((0, 0)\) of \(y = \sqrt[3]{x}\) moves to \((1, 0)\).

blocks.title: Example 11
steps:
Given: the cube root function \(y = \sqrt[3]{x - 1}\).
To find: its domain and range, a table of values and its graph.
Method: decide the domain and range, make a table for \(x = -5\) to \(5\), plot the points and join them with a smooth curve.

Step 1: Domain and range
As we know that cube root function is defined for all real numbers because the cube root of any number (positive, negative or zero) is always real. Therefore, the domain of the given cube root function is all real numbers. The range of the given function is also the set of real numbers.
Why: for example \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\) because \((-2)^{3} = -8\). Unlike a square root, a negative number has a real cube root. And every real \(y\) is reached: \(y = \sqrt[3]{x - 1}\) gives \(x = y^{3} + 1\).

Step 2: Table of values
\[x = 1:\ y = \sqrt[3]{0} = 0\]
\[x = 2:\ y = \sqrt[3]{1} = 1\]
\[x = 0:\ y = \sqrt[3]{-1} = -1\]
\[x = 3:\ y = \sqrt[3]{2} \approx 1.3\]
\[x = -1:\ y = \sqrt[3]{-2} \approx -1.3\]
The remaining values in the table below are found the same way and rounded to one decimal place.
Why: \(x - 1 = 0, 1, -1\) give exact cube roots; the others need a calculator.

Step 3: Plot and join
Plot the points of the table and join them with a smooth curve through \((0, -1)\), \((1, 0)\) and \((2, 1)\) (see the table and graph below).
Why: near \(x = 1\) the values change fastest, so the curve is steepest at \((1, 0)\); far from it the curve flattens but keeps rising.

Check:
\[(-1.8)^{3} \approx -5.8\]
and \(x - 1 = -5 - 1 = -6\); since \(-1.8\) is rounded (\(\sqrt[3]{-6} \approx -1.817\)), this agrees. Also \(1.3^{3} \approx 2.2 \approx 2 = 3 - 1\).
blocks.answer: Domain: all real numbers; range: all real numbers. The graph is the curve through the table points, crossing the \(x\)-axis at \((1, 0)\).

blocks.text: Table values and the graph of the function are given below:

blocks.caption: Table (as printed in the book): values of y = ∛(x − 1), to one decimal place

blocks.alt: Graph of y = cube root of (x minus 1) for x from minus 6 to 6, with the y-axis marked from minus 2 to 2 in steps of 0.5. The curve rises through the table points, passes through (0, minus 1), crosses the x-axis at (1, 0) where it is steepest, and passes through (2, 1); it continues on both sides.
blocks.caption: Figure: graph of y = ∛(x − 1), crossing the x-axis at (1, 0) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(y = \sqrt[3]{x}\): domain and range are all real numbers; negative numbers have negative cube roots.
2. \(y = \sqrt[3]{x - h}\) is \(y = \sqrt[3]{x}\) moved \(h\) units right; it crosses the \(x\)-axis at \((h, 0)\).
3. The graph rises everywhere, is steepest at its centre and flattens far from it.
4. Use values of \(x\) that make \(x - 1\) a perfect cube for exact points.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Treating the cube root like the square root and leaving out negative \(x\): \(\sqrt[3]{-2}\) is real (\(\approx -1.26\)).
2. Dropping the minus sign: \(\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2\), not \(2\).
3. Moving the graph the wrong way: \(x - 1\) inside shifts it to the right, not to the left.
